candidateRows: Objective moral facts do not exist because values reflect human attitudes and practices rather than standards ratified by the universe.
This directly advances the negative side of the motion by defining moral error theory and denying intrinsic or attitude-independent value.
At the outset of his opening statement, Lutz distinguishes subjective valuing from objective value and denies that agents answer to universe-level standards of correctness.
Moral knowledge is impossible because moral beliefs are not formed in response to evidence that gives good reason to regard them as true.
The move directly addresses the epistemic half of the motion by denying moral evidence, justified moral belief, and moral knowledge.
After defining error theory, Lutz introduces moral skepticism and argues that the nonevidential formation of moral beliefs precludes justification and knowledge.
Moral obligations would require desire-independent categorical reasons, but reasons arise from the promotion of desires, so moral obligations do not exist.
This is the principal metaphysical argument for error theory, connecting the concept of moral obligation to allegedly unintelligible categorical normativity.
Lutz contrasts intelligible desire-based reasons, illustrated through drinking coffee to remain awake, with mysterious categorical reasons that would bind regardless of desire.
Evidence supports a belief only when its truth best explains experience, and moral truths do not best explain moral experience, so there is no moral knowledge.
This supplies the negative side's core epistemological argument against moral evidence and directly contests appearance-based justification in the motion.
Lutz explains ordinary perceptual belief through inference to the best explanation, then argues that naturalistic explanations of moral intuitions leave moral truths evidentially idle.
Error theory is less plausible than obvious moral judgments such as that suffering is bad and torturing people for fun is wrong.
The move directly defends moral realism by comparing the plausibility of basic moral appearances with the premises offered for moral anti-realism.
Lutz's opening denial of objective value and his desire-based argument for moral error theory.
Huemer defines objectivity, surveys three anti-realist alternatives, and argues that error theory entails denials of highly plausible elementary moral judgments.
Appearances provide prima facie justification unless defeated, because denying all appearance-based justification would make the denial itself unjustified.
This is the principal positive epistemological thesis supporting moral knowledge by appearances and directly opposes explanationism as the exclusive evidential standard.
Lutz's claim that beliefs are justified only when their truth belongs to the best explanation of experience.
Huemer states a defeasible appearance principle and argues that philosophical beliefs themselves rest on how matters seem, making wholesale rejection self-undermining.
Desires alone cannot explain rational action because judgments about which present, future, or imagined desires to follow depend on evaluative facts.
This attacks the decisive premise of the con side's metaphysical case by arguing that rational discrimination among desires presupposes genuine evaluative judgments.
Lutz's premise that every reason for action derives from an agent's desires, goals, or values.
Using the partying student, Odysseus and the sirens, charitable giving, and needed surgery, Huemer argues that desire-based decision rules alternate between rational and irrational results.
Without truth-valued evaluative facts, error theory cannot explain why consistency and coherence should matter for an agent's values or desires.
The argument supports realism by contending that a familiar standard for assessing values has no rationale if evaluative attitudes lack truth or falsity.
The error-theoretic position that values are merely attitudes rather than responses to objective evaluative facts.
Huemer contrasts beliefs, whose inconsistency guarantees falsity, with desires, which can be unlikely or impossible to satisfy without thereby becoming irrational.
The Humean argument validly opposes moral facts to desire-dependent reasons, and choosing between it and realism ultimately depends on the comparative appeal of whole worldviews.
This restates the con side's central metaphysical inference and answers the realist objection that the argument should be rejected because realism is independently plausible.
Huemer's objection that moral realism is more plausible than the Humean premise restricting reasons to desires.
Lutz formally reconstructs the Humean argument, acknowledges the clash of starting points, and frames rational assessment as comparison between broader philosophical outlooks.
Cases of overpowering desires do not refute desire-based reasons because normative weight tracks a desire's centrality to the agent's self-conception, not motivational strength.
This is the con side's detailed defense of the desire-based theory against Huemer's principal counterexamples, preserving the premise that supports error theory.
Huemer's partying-student and Odysseus examples, offered to show that desires cannot determine an agent's normative reasons.
Lutz rejects simple proportionalism and argues that identity-central projects explain why studying or surviving can provide stronger reasons than immediately overwhelming impulses.
Error theory should be rejected because its denial that gratuitous torture is wrong is less initially plausible than the moral judgment it conflicts with.
This directly defends objective morality by making the comparative plausibility of a paradigmatic moral judgment decisive against error theory.
The error-theoretic claim that normative reasons ultimately derive from an agent's desires.
After the opposing account distinguishes desire strength from reason strength, Huemer returns to the core dispute and invokes a highly evident moral prohibition.
Centrality to self-conception does not explain rational authority, since ordinary weakness of will and arbitrary higher-order desires can occur without such centrality.
The move attacks the proposed replacement for proportionalism through ordinary counterexamples and challenges its ability to distinguish rationally authoritative desires.
Lutz's proposal that a desire's normative weight depends on its centrality to the agent's self-conception.
Huemer uses the marshmallow test, weakness of will, an irrational self-conception, and arbitrary second-order desires to pressure the revised Humean account.
A desire's momentary motivational force need not determine its normative strength because rational reflection can criticize compulsions that are alien to the agent's deeper self.
This supplies the principal error-theoretic defense against weakness-of-will counterexamples while preserving a desire-based account of normative reasons.
Huemer's and the moderator's objections that self-conception is arbitrary and fails to ground stronger reasons.
Lutz distinguishes having a reason from its strength and argues that reflective agency can reject unusually forceful passing desires as alien compulsions.
The Humean account cannot assign intrinsic importance to self-conception without explaining that importance through desire, and it cannot dismiss desires merely because they arise externally.
The argument alleges that the revised theory either abandons its desire-based foundation or lacks a principled way to rank desires by their origins.
Lutz's claim that rational criticism reflects a deeper self whose central desires possess greater normative authority.
Huemer presses for a theoretical ground of self-centrality and argues that biological, cultural, and cultivated desires all have unchosen external causal sources.
Normative reasons must resonate with an agent's goals, values, and deliberative perspective because wholly disconnected demands would be alienating and unable to guide action intelligibly.
This is the most developed theoretical grounding offered for the Humean view and explains why agent-relative desires confer rational authority.
Huemer's demand for a theoretical explanation of why differences among desires should normatively matter.
Lutz relaxes a strict motivational constraint but maintains that reasons must connect with the standpoint from which agents deliberate and pursue worthy-seeming goals.
Abandoning belief in objective moral facts would substantially alter many people's desires, emotions, charitable conduct, and interpretation of ordinary actions.
The move challenges the practical adequacy of error theory by arguing that moral beliefs help constitute motivations rather than merely overlay independent desires.
Lutz's contention that people would continue living by their desires even if they recognized that no moral facts existed.
Huemer predicts greater selfishness without moral realism and explains that many ordinary motivations are partly formed by beliefs about rightness, wrongness, and value.
Moral belief is largely a projection of prior values onto the world, so removing belief in objective morality would usually leave the underlying attitudes and behavior intact.
This explains both the origin of widespread moral belief under error theory and why rejecting objective facts need not eliminate moralized conduct.
Huemer's claim that moral beliefs partly generate desires and that losing realism would radically alter common behavior.
Lutz characterizes moral judgment as a cognitive projection of values and limits major behavioral change to unusual agents who act from duty without corresponding concern.
Intellectual moral judgments can override stronger emotional attractions, and moral beliefs commonly shape the emotions that motivate intervention in perceived injustice.
The argument disputes the claimed priority of desire by offering cases where judgment directs conduct and helps determine the relevant emotional response.
Lutz's projection account and his claim that independent underlying attitudes would normally preserve conduct without moral belief.
Huemer contrasts cost-effective charity with emotional appeal and argues that changing beliefs about who is right in a conflict can dissolve indignation and motivation.
Psychological evidence indicates that emotions generally cause moral judgments, while apparently unemotional deliberation still reflects stable cold passions tied to self-conception.
This gives empirical and conceptual support for the desire-first explanation and absorbs calm intellectual choice into the same motivational framework.
Huemer's claim that evaluative judgments often generate emotions and motivate choices independently of stronger emotional attractions.
Lutz appeals to social-intuitionist research, describes his own unchanged conduct as an error theorist, and treats settled concerns as cold rather than absent passions.
Emotion-first studies may not generalize to central moral judgments, and even when emotion precedes judgment, defeating the judgment can undermine both the emotion and resulting behavior.
The move weakens the empirical basis for desire-first error theory and preserves a substantial causal role for cognition in moral motivation.
Lutz's appeal to social-intuitionist evidence that emotions generally drive moral judgments rather than the reverse.
Huemer questions whether unusual experimental prompts represent obvious moral cases and argues that cognition can precede emotion unconsciously or later revise it.
Explaining apparently judgment-guided altruism by invoking an unseen cold desire threatens to make the desire-based theory unfalsifiable.
The objection tests whether the con side's desire-grounded account has empirical content when counterexamples can always be redescribed as cold passions.
Lutz's appeal to cold passions as the motivational basis of apparently judgment-guided conduct.
After discussing how corrected beliefs can alter emotions and behavior, Huemer uses effective charitable giving to press the falsifiability of Lutz's motivational account.
Effective altruistic reasoning can rationally select a means while still being motivationally launched by an initial emotional concern for others.
The response preserves the con account by separating rational means selection from the emotional concern that supplies the motivating end.
Huemer's claim that effective altruism appears guided by judgment rather than emotion or desire.
Lutz answers the effective-altruist example by distinguishing concern about suffering from the later calculation that identifies the most effective intervention.
Experience supports belief through background causal understanding rather than by possessing propositional content that directly confers justification.
This is the con side's central epistemological alternative to appearance-based prima facie justification and directly addresses the motion's knowledge question.
Huemer's intuitionist view that an experience with propositional content directly provides prima facie justification.
Asked to identify his problem with intuitionism, Lutz questions experiential propositional content and explains perceptual justification through causally structured cognition.
Causal and best-explanation reasoning cannot get started unless agents initially accept that things are generally as they appear to be.
The move directly argues that appearance-based justification is epistemically prior to, and indispensable for, any best-explanation framework.
Lutz's claim that background causal beliefs explain why experiences justify perceptual beliefs without direct seeming-based warrant.
Huemer first clarifies experiential content, then argues that concepts, causal beliefs, and judgments of explanatory quality ultimately depend on initially trusting appearances.
Predictive refinement can generate sophisticated concepts and reliable causal models without beginning from contentful experiences accepted as true.
The predictive-processing model supplies the con side's substantive answer to Huemer's regress challenge against explanationist epistemology.
Huemer's argument that causal and explanatory beliefs must be bootstrapped by initially accepting contentful appearances.
Lutz appeals cautiously to machine learning and empirical predictive-processing models to explain how largely unstructured systems acquire complex causal organization.
AI has no intrinsic mental representation, while human perceptual concepts arise only after genuine contentful experiences represent worldly objects.
The reply challenges the key analogy supporting Lutz's non-foundational account and reinstates contentful experience as prior to worldly concepts.
Lutz's predictive-processing analogy between AI learning and the human acquisition of concepts and causal models.
Huemer denies that computer data intrinsically represents anything and argues that once genuine human mental states arise, perceptual belief depends on prior represented experience.
Mathematical reflection provides experiential evidence by indicating correct conceptual application and relations, not through intellectual seemings with mathematical propositions as content.
The account extends explanationism to an apparent paradigm of a priori seeming-based knowledge and therefore answers a major challenge to the con epistemology.
The challenge that mathematical truths such as two plus two equals four are justified by overwhelmingly powerful intellectual seemings.
Lutz accepts that mathematical thought has an experiential aspect but interprets confidence as evidence about concept use and concept relations within a quasi-experimental process.
Necessary a priori truths such as the incompatibility of being wholly red and wholly blue appear synthetic because synonym substitution cannot reduce them to logical truths.
The examples pressure the empiricist restriction of a priori knowledge to analytic truths and support Huemer's broader rationalist epistemology.
Lutz's empiricist claim that mathematical truths are conceptual and that reflective experience reveals relations among concepts.
Huemer invokes color incompatibility and causal priority as putative synthetic a priori truths that resist a narrow synonym-substitution account of analyticity.
Color incompatibility is analytic on a broader conception because familiarity with phenomenal color concepts manifests an understanding that their all-over application is inconsistent.
The reply seeks to absorb Huemer's synthetic-a-priori counterexample into empiricism by replacing the narrow account of analyticity with a phenomenal-concept account.
Huemer's contention that wholly red and wholly blue cannot coincide is a synthetic rather than analytic a priori truth.
Lutz argues that knowing red and blue experiences suffices to grasp their incompatibility, while conceding that he has not yet fully formulated the better theory of analyticity.
A priori knowledge concerns the natures of things rather than merely words or concepts, and understanding badness and suffering can therefore justify the judgment that suffering is bad.
The closing integrates the dispute over explanation, analyticity, synthetic a priori knowledge, and ethical intuition into the pro side's answer to the motion.
Lutz's explanationist rejection of objective morality and his empiricist attempt to classify all a priori knowledge as analytic.
Huemer summarizes agreement against ethical naturalism, rejects explanation as a universal condition of justification, distinguishes things from concepts, and extends rationalism to moral knowledge.
